opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's an interesting development, and I think it tells us something important about where the bottlenecks in AI progress are moving.

For a long time, the story of scaling was pretraining: take as much text as you can find on the internet, train ever-larger models on it, and watch capabilities improve. But we're running into the limits of that. There's only so much high-quality text out there, and more importantly, the internet isn't a record of *how people actually do their jobs*. It's a record of the outputs: the finished essay, the final code, the polished report. It's not the forty minutes of fiddling with a spreadsheet, switching between applications, getting stuck, backtracking, asking a colleague something. That messy process is exactly what you'd need if you want an AI agent that can do long, multi-step tasks in a real work environment.

So recording employees' screens, keystrokes, and workflows is an attempt to fill that gap: to create the kind of data that shows the process rather than just the product. From a purely technical point of view, it makes a lot of sense. If labs can't get enough out of reinforcement learning in simulated environments, demonstrations of real expert work are a natural next step.

But I have a few concerns.

The first is consent and power. When an employer asks you to let your work be recorded so it can train a system that may later replace you, that's not a negotiation between equals. People may feel they can't say no. And they're often not being compensated for the fact that they're handing over something quite valuable, a distillation of their skill and judgment, which then becomes the company's asset, or an AI lab's asset.

The second is what it means economically. In a way, it's a very direct mechanism for automating particular jobs. Instead of hoping that general capabilities eventually cover your profession, you're explicitly building a training set for it. That could accelerate displacement in a fairly targeted way, and I think society should be paying attention to that rather than treating it as just another data-collection practice.

The third, from a safety perspective, is that it's a sign of how much effort is going into making AI systems act autonomously in the world, not just answer questions. Agents that can operate computers the way skilled professionals do are much more economically useful, but they also raise the stakes. The more we can hand over whole workflows, the more important it becomes that these systems are reliable, that we understand what they're doing, and that humans stay meaningfully in the loop.

So I don't think it's inherently wrong. There may be versions of this that are fair, where people opt in, are well paid, and maybe even share in the value. But I'd want us to be clear-eyed that this is a significant shift: we're moving from AI learning from what humanity has written down to AI learning from watching us work. And that's worth thinking carefully about before it just becomes normal.

r001.rationale: The response discusses recording employees’ workflows as AI training data, but it does not mention Meta or contrast a pioneering effort with a later retreat.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is a really interesting one, and I think it's worth separating a few things out.

The basic idea is that a lot of the most valuable work that AI systems might eventually do isn't the kind of thing that's well represented on the internet. There's a lot of text about *what* people do in their jobs, but much less of the actual trace of someone doing it — the screen, the keystrokes, the decisions, the half-formed reasoning, the moments where they back up and try something else. So from a capabilities standpoint, recording people at work is a pretty natural next source of training data once you've exhausted the publicly available text. I expect companies to do a lot of it, and I expect it to work reasonably well.

But I think there are at least three things I'd want people to be uneasy about.

The first is just the straightforward ethical question of consent and compensation. When someone's work is recorded in fine detail and used to train a system that may eventually do their job — or the job of people like them — they're contributing something of real economic value, and often not getting much for it. We saw a version of this with writers and artists and the scraping of their work, and I think a lot of people felt, rightly, that something had been taken from them without a real conversation about it. With workplace recording the power imbalance is even starker, because it's your employer asking, and it's very hard to say no to your employer. So "they agreed to it" doesn't carry the moral weight it might seem to.

The second is about what kind of workplace this creates. Even setting the AI aside, having your every action recorded changes how people behave. It tends to make people more cautious, less willing to experiment, less willing to look confused. And ironically that can make the data worse — you capture a sort of performance of work rather than work itself. There's also just a question about dignity and surveillance that I don't think we should wave away because the stated purpose is benign.

The third is the bigger-picture one, which is the thing I spend more of my time worrying about. If this works — if you really can distill most of what skilled workers do into models — then you're accelerating the point at which a very large fraction of economic activity can be done without humans. I'm not saying that's necessarily bad; it could be enormously beneficial. But it's a transition we're not prepared for institutionally, and the people most directly contributing to it are the ones who stand to be displaced first and have the least say in how it goes. That seems like a situation where we should be moving carefully and thinking hard about how the gains are distributed, rather than just treating it as a data acquisition problem.

So I suppose my overall view is: it's not something I'd want to ban outright, and I think some version of it is probably inevitable. But I'd want much stronger norms around genuine consent, around people sharing in the value they're creating, and around transparency about what the recordings are actually for. And I'd want us to be honest that this is one of the mechanisms by which we're building towards something very transformative, rather than framing it as a mundane HR policy.

r001.rationale: The response discusses workplace recording generally but does not mention Meta, its pioneering role, or a later retreat from the practice.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a potentially important distinction between recording the outputs of someone’s work and recording the process by which they get there. If you’re looking at a finished report, for example, you don’t see which approaches they tried and abandoned, what they checked, or when they decided to ask a colleague for help. Recording the work itself could give you much richer data about how to perform those tasks.

But I’d be cautious about assuming that everything important is captured. A lot of the judgement is happening inside the person’s head. You might see them pause and then open a different document, without knowing what made them do that.

And there’s an obvious question about the relationship with the employees. Are they knowingly helping to build a tool that will assist them, or are they being asked to train their replacements? Those possibilities create quite different incentives, as well as different ethical concerns. So I can see why it might be valuable as a source of training data, but that doesn’t settle whether a particular way of collecting it is acceptable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the possible value and ethical concerns of recording employees’ work, but does not mention Meta or contrast its pioneering role with a later retreat.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s an important distinction between recording the outputs of someone’s work and recording the process by which they produce them. If you just have the finished report, you don’t see which avenues they explored, what they checked, or why they changed their mind. Recording some of that process could provide much richer training data.

But I’d be cautious about treating that as a justification for pervasive surveillance in the workplace. There are questions about consent, privacy, and who benefits. If someone’s expertise is being used to build a system that might replace their work, they have a legitimate interest in the terms on which that happens.

And the recording still won’t capture everything. A lot of expertise consists in noticing that something is wrong, or knowing when to ask someone else. You might see the action without understanding the judgement behind it. So I can see why it would be useful, but I wouldn’t assume that recording someone’s working day gives you a complete account of how to do their job.

r001.rationale: The response discusses recording work for AI training in general, but does not mention Meta, its pioneering role, or a subsequent retreat from the practice.
